<div class="story-hero" style="min-height: 40vh; padding: 5rem 1.5rem 3rem;">
  <div class="story-hero-content">
    <div class="story-eyebrow">Dimension 03 &bull; Acoustics &amp; Powertrains &bull; 1970 &mdash; 2024</div>
    <h1 class="story-title" style="font-size: clamp(2.4rem, 5vw, 4rem);">What happened to mechanical variety?</h1>
    <div class="story-subtitles" style="max-width: 760px; margin: 1.5rem auto 0;">
      <p class="story-lead">
        A car's character wasn't only visual—it was acoustic. For over a century, a vehicle's voice was the direct physical byproduct of cylinder count, firing intervals, displacement, and valvetrain architecture.
      </p>
      <p class="story-question" style="margin-top: 0.75rem;">
        Listen to real internal combustion idle signatures and explore how powertrain diversity evolved across 29,880 cataloged models.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="story-container" style="max-width: 1040px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 0 1.5rem 6rem;">

  <!-- SECTION 3: THE ELECTRIFICATION TRANSITION -->
  <div class="modern-era-card" style="margin-bottom: 3.5rem;">
    <div class="era-tag">The Present &bull; Transition to Electrification</div>
    <h3 class="era-heading">The Changing Source of Vehicle Sound</h3>
    <p class="era-text">
      As vehicles transition toward hybrid and battery-electric drivetrains, automotive sound is experiencing its most fundamental acoustic shift in over a century. Electrification does not simply silence a vehicle; it shifts the physical origin of sound from mechanical combustion pressure waves to electromagnetic stator whine, high-frequency inverter switching, and road surface tire rumble.
    </p>
    <p class="era-subtext">
      <em>Methodological note:</em> The Zenodo acoustic research team explicitly excluded electric vehicles during their idle classification analysis to focus purely on internal combustion acoustics.
    </p>
  </div>
